tips.title: There are only four sums to learn
tips.body: **0+0 = 0**, **0+1 = 1**, **1+1 = 10** (write 0, carry 1), **1+1+1 = 11** (write 1, carry 1). That is the whole of binary addition. The last one only comes up when you are adding three numbers, which is exactly when it is needed.

tips.title: Check by converting
tips.body: Convert both numbers to decimal, add them, and convert the answer back. If it does not match your binary working, you have made a carry mistake. It costs thirty seconds and catches nearly every error in this topic.

tips.title: A ninth bit means overflow
tips.body: The specification keeps answers to **8 bits**. If a carry comes out of the leftmost column there is nowhere to put it, and that is an **overflow error** — the result is too large for the space available. Say the words "overflow error"; "it goes wrong" earns nothing.

tips.title: Shifting right loses what falls off
tips.body: A right shift of an **odd** number loses the 1 in the units column for ever. `00010111` (23) shifted right once is `00001011` = 11, **not** 11.5. It is division by 2 that throws away any remainder.

tips.title: Only logical shifts are examined
tips.body: AQA asks for the **logical** shift only: bits move, **zeros come in** at the empty end, and whatever falls off the other end is lost. You do not need arithmetic shifts, and you do not need fractions.

why.matters:
A processor cannot multiply, divide or compare in any direct sense. It can **add**, and it can **shift bits sideways**, and everything else is built out of those two — which is why they are worth doing by hand once.

It is also where the limits of a machine come from. Eight bits hold 0 to 255 and no more, so a sum that goes past it has nowhere to put the answer. That is not a mistake in the arithmetic; it is **overflow**, and real systems have failed because of it.

examples.title: Why a counter can go round to zero
examples.body:
Eight bits reach **255** and stop. Add 200 and 100 in eight bits and the answer needs a ninth, and there is no ninth column to put it in.

The carry is simply lost, and the stored answer is wrong — quietly, with no error message. That is **overflow**, and it is why a game score can wrap back to zero, and why the number of bits a program uses for a value is a design decision rather than a detail.

visual.alt: A table of how far a fixed number of bits can count: four bits reach fifteen, eight reach two hundred and fifty-five and sixteen reach sixty-five thousand five hundred and thirty-five, and one more sends each back to zero

examples.title: Why shifting left is multiplying
examples.body:
Move every bit one place to the left, put a zero in at the right, and the value **doubles**: 23 becomes 46. Shift right and it **halves**: 23 becomes 11.

It works for the same reason moving a decimal digit left multiplies by ten — each place is worth twice the one to its right. A processor can shift far more cheaply than it can multiply, so multiplying by a power of two is done this way wherever speed matters. And notice what the right shift cost: the odd 1 fell off the end and is gone for good.

visual.alt: A table showing a logical shift: twenty-three in binary shifted one place left becomes forty-six, and shifted one place right becomes eleven, the odd bit falling off the end

examples.title: Why you check by converting
examples.body:
Binary addition has only four column sums to learn, and every one of them is easy. The marks are lost in the **carries**, which is a bookkeeping problem rather than an understanding one.

So there is a check that costs ten seconds and needs no confidence: convert both numbers to decimal, add them there, convert your binary answer back, and see whether the two agree. It catches a dropped carry without your knowing where it was — which is the best kind of check, and the same trick as the mass check in a chemical equation.

visual.alt: A table of the four binary column sums: nought plus nought is nought, nought plus one is one, one plus one writes nought and carries one, and one plus one plus one writes one and carries one

steps.title: Adding binary numbers
steps.body:
**Binary addition works exactly like decimal addition — start at the right, carry when a column overflows.** The only difference is that a column overflows at 2 rather than at 10.

**The four sums:**

| Column | Write | Carry |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 + 0 | 0 | – |
| 0 + 1 | 1 | – |
| **1 + 1** | **0** | **1** |
| **1 + 1 + 1** | **1** | **1** |

The third is the one that catches people: 1 + 1 is **10** in binary, so you write 0 and carry 1 — just as 5 + 5 makes you write 0 and carry 1 in decimal.

The fourth only appears when adding **three** numbers. 1 + 1 + 1 is **11** in binary, which is 3, so you write 1 and carry 1.

**What the specification limits you to:**

- adding up to **three** binary numbers
- a maximum of **8 bits** per number
- at most **three 1s in a single column**
- answers of at most **8 bits**, with no carry past the eighth

So you will never be asked to add four numbers, and a correct answer will always fit in a byte.

check.solution: Working right to left with the carries gives **01010000**. Check: $58 + 22 = 80$, and `01010000` is $64 + 16 = 80$ ✓

steps.title: Adding three numbers, and overflow
steps.body:
**Adding three numbers brings in the fourth column sum.** When three 1s land in one column, 1 + 1 + 1 = **11** in binary, so you **write 1 and carry 1**.

Adding `00001111`, `00000011`, `00000101`:

The units column has **three 1s** — write 1, carry 1. Working the rest through gives `00010111`, and the check confirms it: 15 + 3 + 5 = **23**, and `00010111` = 16 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 23.

The specification says you will never meet **more** than three 1s in a column, so those four sums are all you ever need.

**Overflow.** Eight bits hold 0 to 255. If a carry comes out of the leftmost column there is **nowhere to put it**, because the byte has no ninth bit:

`11111111` + `00000001` would need `100000000` — **9 bits**.

That is an **overflow error**: the result is too large for the space available. The name is what earns the mark. In a real computer the ninth bit is simply lost, so the stored answer comes out as 0 — right arithmetic, wrong answer, which is why overflow matters.

In the exam, the specification promises answers will **not** carry beyond the eighth bit, so overflow is something you explain rather than something you have to work around.

steps.title: Binary shifts
steps.body:
**A logical binary shift moves every bit the same number of places.** Zeros fill the empty end, and anything pushed off the other end is **lost**.

**Shifting left multiplies by 2 for each place.** `00010110` (22) shifted **left 2** becomes `01011000` = 88, and 22 × 4 = 88. Two places is × 2², which is × 4.

**Shifting right divides by 2 for each place.** `00010110` (22) shifted **right 1** becomes `00001011` = 11, and 22 ÷ 2 = 11.

**Bits that fall off are gone.** This matters when the number is **odd**. `00010111` is 23; shift right once and the 1 in the units column drops off the end, giving `00001011` = **11**, not 11.5. A right shift is division by 2 that **throws away the remainder**. The specification is clear that you do not need fractional representations, so this is the expected behaviour, not a failure.

The same loss happens shifting **left** if a 1 is pushed off the top: the value is no longer what the multiplication should give.

**Why computers do this.** A shift is a very cheap operation — far cheaper than a general multiply or divide — so multiplying or dividing by a power of 2 is done with a shift wherever possible.

**Only logical shifts are examined**: bits move, zeros come in, what falls off is lost.

check.prompt: What is the effect of shifting a binary number two places to the left?
options: It multiplies the number by 4
It multiplies the number by 2
It divides the number by 4
It adds 2 to the number
check.solution: Each place left multiplies by 2, so two places is $2^2 = $ **× 4**.

steps.title: Your turn
steps.body:
**Part A.**

1. Give the four binary column sums, with the carry for each.
2. How many binary numbers can you be asked to add at once?
3. What is the largest number of 1s the specification allows in one column?

**Part B.**

4. Add `00101101` and `00010011`.
5. Add `00001111`, `00000011` and `00000101`.
6. Shift `00010110` two places left and give the decimal value before and after.

**Part C.**

7. Shift `00010111` one place right. Explain why the answer is not exactly half of the original.
8. Explain what an overflow error is and when one occurs.
9. Explain why a computer might use a shift instead of a multiplication.

Check questions 4 and 5 by converting to decimal and adding.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Always check by converting.** Add the two decimal values, convert your binary answer back, and see that they agree. Carry errors are the main way marks are lost here, and this catches nearly all of them in under a minute.

**Work right to left, and write the carries down.** A carry held in your head is a carry that gets dropped, usually three columns later.

**Name the error: "overflow".** A question asking what happens when a result needs a ninth bit wants the words **overflow error** — the result is too large for the number of bits available. *It goes wrong* or *the answer is too big* will not do. It is worth adding what actually happens: the extra bit is **lost**, so `11111111` + 1 stores as `00000000`, which looks like 0.

**Be exact about shifts.** A left shift of $n$ places multiplies by $2^n$; a right shift divides by $2^n$. *Doubles it* is only true for one place, and a question usually asks for two or three.

**Say what falls off.** The full answer on a right shift of an odd number is that the 1 in the units column is **pushed out and lost**, so `00010111` (23) becomes 11 and not 11.5. A right shift is integer division: the remainder is discarded. The specification says fractional representations are not required, so this is intended behaviour.

**Remember a left shift can lose data too.** Push a 1 off the top of the byte and the result is no longer the multiplication you wanted. Most students only mention loss on right shifts.

**Know why shifts are used.** They are a much cheaper operation than a general multiply or divide, so a computer uses a shift whenever it is multiplying or dividing by a power of 2.

**Only the logical shift is examined.** Bits move, **zeros** enter the vacated end, what falls off is gone. Arithmetic shifts and fractions are outside the specification.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- Binary addition works like decimal, but a column overflows at **2**.
- **0+0 = 0**, **0+1 = 1**, **1+1 = 10** (write 0, carry 1), **1+1+1 = 11** (write 1, carry 1).
- Work **right to left** and write each carry down.
- The specification allows up to **three** numbers, **8 bits** each, at most **three 1s** in a column.
- Answers are at most **8 bits**, with no carry past the eighth.
- **Check by converting** to decimal and adding.
- A carry out of the leftmost column is an **overflow error**.
- Overflow means the result is **too large for the bits available**; the extra bit is lost.
- A **logical shift** moves every bit; **zeros** fill the empty end.
- Whatever is pushed off the end is **lost**.
- **Left** by $n$ places **multiplies** by $2^n$.
- **Right** by $n$ places **divides** by $2^n$.
- `00010110` left 2 = `01011000`, so 22 × 4 = 88.
- A right shift of an **odd** number loses its units bit: 23 becomes 11, not 11.5.
- Shifts are used because they are **cheaper** than multiply and divide.

questions.prompt: Explain how binary addition works, including what happens when a column holds three 1s and what an overflow error is.
questions.solution:
Binary addition works in the same way as decimal addition: you line the numbers up, start at the **right-hand column**, and carry into the next column whenever the total is too large for one digit. The only difference is that a binary column overflows at **2** rather than at 10.

There are only four column sums to know. **0 + 0** writes 0. **0 + 1** writes 1. **1 + 1** is **10** in binary, so you write **0 and carry 1** — exactly as 5 + 5 makes you write 0 and carry 1 in decimal. A carry coming in from the right joins its column like any other 1.

**Three 1s in a column** happens when three numbers are added, or when a carry lands in a column that already has two 1s. 1 + 1 + 1 is **11** in binary, which is 3, so you **write 1 and carry 1**. The specification limits questions to three numbers of at most eight bits each, so three 1s is the most that can ever appear in one column and those four sums are all that is needed.

Adding `00111010` and `00010110` gives `01010000`, which can be checked by converting: $58 + 22 = 80$, and `01010000` is $64 + 16 = 80$. That conversion check takes under a minute and catches almost every carry mistake.

An **overflow error** occurs when the result of a calculation is **too large for the number of bits available**. In an eight-bit system the largest value is 255, so adding 1 to `11111111` gives 256, which is `100000000` — **nine** bits. There is no ninth bit in a byte, so the extra bit is **lost** and `00000000` is stored. The arithmetic was carried out correctly and the stored answer is nevertheless 0, which is precisely why overflow is a problem worth naming: the computer gives no warning, and a program that does not check for it carries on with a wrong value.

In this specification, exam additions are promised not to carry beyond the eighth bit, so overflow is something to **explain** rather than to work around. If an answer needs nine bits, a mistake has been made earlier.

questions.prompt: Explain what a logical binary shift does, the effect it has on a number's value, and when data can be lost.
questions.solution:
A **logical binary shift** moves every bit in a number the same number of places, either left or right. **Zeros** fill the positions vacated at the end the bits moved away from, and any bit pushed off the opposite end is **lost**. The number of bits stays the same throughout — the byte does not grow to make room. AQA examines the logical shift only; arithmetic shifts and fractional representations are not required.

**The effect on the value** follows from the place values doubling at each step. A shift **left** of $n$ places **multiplies** the number by $2^n$, and a shift **right** of $n$ places **divides** it by $2^n$. So `00010110` is 22, and shifting it two places left gives `01011000` = 88, which is $22 \times 4$. Shifting it one place right gives `00001011` = 11, which is $22 \div 2$. It is worth being precise here: *it doubles it* is only true for a shift of **one** place, and questions usually ask for two or three.

This is why shifts are used at all. A shift is a very **cheap** operation for the hardware, much cheaper than a general multiply or divide, so a computer performs multiplication and division by a **power of 2** with a shift wherever it can. It only works for powers of 2, which is the limitation.

**Data can be lost in both directions**, and this is where most answers stop half way.

Shifting **right** loses the bits that fall off the right-hand end. This matters for an **odd** number, which has a 1 in the units column. `00010111` is 23; shifted right once it becomes `00001011` = **11**, not 11.5. A right shift is therefore **integer division**: the remainder is discarded and cannot be recovered.

Shifting **left** can lose data too. If a 1 is pushed off the **left-hand** end of the byte it is gone, and the result is no longer the multiplication that was intended — the value comes out far smaller than it should. Because of this, shifts are **not reversible**: shifting 23 right twice gives 5, and shifting that back left twice gives 20, not 23. A shift can only be undone when nothing was lost in the first place.

markScheme.description: multiply and divide by powers of 2

examTechnique.body:
Work **right to left** and write every carry above its column. Then **check by converting**: add the decimal values and convert your answer back.

Name **overflow** when a result needs a ninth bit. For shifts, say **multiplies by $2^n$** rather than "doubles it", and say what **falls off the end**.
examinerErrors: Holding carries in your head and dropping one.
Writing 2 in a column instead of carrying.
Getting 1 + 1 + 1 wrong — it writes 1 and carries 1.
Saying "it goes wrong" instead of naming an overflow error.
Saying a shift of two places "doubles" the number.
Assuming only right shifts can lose data.
Giving an answer longer than eight bits.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer writes the carries down, works right to left, and **checks by converting** before moving on. It names an **overflow error** in those words and adds what is actually stored — the ninth bit is lost, so `11111111` + 1 reads as 0. On shifts it says **multiplies by $2^n$**, not "doubles", and it explains loss in **both** directions: the units bit of an odd number falling off a right shift, and a 1 falling off the top of a left shift. It knows a shift is used because it is **cheaper** than a multiply, and that shifts are not reversible once a bit has gone.
